title: Temporal Carveout and Soft-Threshold Arbiter PRD Proposal
body:
Summary:

This PRD proposes a feature set we’re calling Temporal Carveouts + Soft-Threshold Arbiter (TCSA). The goal is to give Dedicated customers predictable short-term burst capacity while preserving tenant isolation and latency SLOs. TCSA combines time-windowed reserved carveouts, a soft admission controller that phases traffic when global headroom is low, and an emergency fallback routing policy so we can offer attractive burst options without increasing noisy-neighbor risk.

Why this is needed (problem statement):
- Customers with spiky workloads want short-duration guaranteed capacity above their monthly reserve (e.g., marketing campaign spikes, end-of-period batch inference). Current burst implementations either: a) offer blunt overcommit that risks tail latency for others, or b) require manual, pre-provisioned hot pools (expensive and operationally heavy).
- Engineering/ops needs a single predictable, observable mechanism that: enforces isolation, offers controlled burst windows, and degrades gracefully when capacity is constrained.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Product: Provide customers with an on-demand "temporal carveout" option (X minutes/hour) that can be purchased or earned, surfaced as an SLA-like contract (e.g., +20% QPS for up to 10 minutes, 4x/day).
- Reliability: Maintain per-tenant P99 and system-wide P99 degradation within agreed limits (target: <5% P99 violations attributable to burst activation).
- Economics: Keep incremental cost of offering carveouts under a threshold (target: <= 1.2x effective token cost during bursts).
- Ops: Provide clear telemetry (carveout usage, admission declines, failovers) and a simple rollback path.

Non-goals:
- This is not a replacement for long-term reserved capacity or Dedicated commit plans.
- Not intended for unbounded polyglot/preemptible workloads.

High level design:
1) Temporal Carveouts (TC):
- Each tenant can hold 0..N carveout entitlements. An entitlement defines: duration (minutes), capacity multiplier (e.g., +30% QPS), and frequency (per day/week).
- Carveouts are implemented as a short-lived reservation of worker capacity: when activated, the system pins a fraction of pool slots (or soft-weights them) for the tenant for the carveout duration.
- Two implementation modes: "hard-lease" (isolated slots pinned; strict guarantee) and "soft-lease" (priority weighted scheduling; strong expectation but preemptible).

2) Soft-Threshold Arbiter (STA):
- STA sits at the admission layer and evaluates: current headroom, active carveouts, latency budgets, and tenant priority.
- When global utilization approaches threshold T_warn (e.g., 75%), STA shifts incoming carveout activations to a phased admission: allow small fraction immediately, queue remainder into a short defer window (seconds to a minute) and try gradual ramping.
- If utilization exceeds hard-threshold T_hard (e.g., 92%), STA can: a) refuse new carveout activations, b) reduce soft-lease weights, c) trigger cross-pool failover to a lower fidelity model or region (policy-controlled).

3) Isolation Controls:
- Latency Budget Fence: every tenant has a rolling latency budget derived from baseline SLO. STA keeps a ledger of budget consumption attributable to bursts; if budget is exhausted, admissions are curtailed until budget replenishes.
- Tenant Penalty Meter: track metric of how often a tenant’s bursts cause global SLO regressions; repeated offenders can be throttled or downgraded to soft-lease-only.
- Shoreline Windows: pre-scheduled windows (e.g., nightly batch) where carveouts are disabled to protect maintenance windows and capacity lead-ins.

Operational model and signals:
- Telemetry emitted per activation: tenant id, entitlement id, requested multiplier, actual allocated slots, admission decision, time-to-fully-ramped, observed P50/P95/P99 impact on pool.
- Alerting: auto open incident if fleet-wide P99 increases > 10% within 10m of carveout activations or if STA refuses > 5% of activations in a 30m window.
- Reconciliation job: nightly job that evaluates carveout economics and suggests pricing adjustments based on observed uplift/cost.

API/UX:
- Admin API: POST /tenants/{id}/carveouts to create entitlements; fields: duration, multiplier, mode (hard/soft), frequency cap.
- Activation endpoint: POST /tenants/{id}/carveouts/{eid}/activate with optional priority tag and fallback preference (model downgrade, region failover, or queue).
- Console: per-tenant carveout usage dashboard, heatmap of activation times, and a "what-if" simulator to preview how a requested carveout would be admitted under current utilization.

Autoscaling interaction:
- Autoscaler stays primary source of long-term capacity decisions. TCSA delegates to autoscaler to provision ephemeral warm-pool candidates when a carveout is accepted and sustained > threshold time (e.g., 120s).
- Short bursts (< threshold) rely on existing headroom + STA admission shaping. For sustained bursts that become long-tail, system proposes converting the entitlement activation into a temporary reserved allocation (promote to short-term reserve) and bill accordingly.

Pricing model (sketch):
- On-demand carveout: flat premium per entitlement activation + per-token surcharge while active.
- Earned carveouts: loyalty-based small customers can earn N soft-carveouts per month based on usage patterns.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (internal alpha): simulate carveouts in staging, run controlled experiments with internal tenants; monitor P99 impact.
- Phase 1 (private beta): offer soft-lease carveouts to selected customers with strict guardrails (lower multipliers, automatic rollback).
- Phase 2 (public beta): enable both soft and hard modes; expose console planner and pricing.
- Phase 3 (GA): full productized entitlements, SLA wording, legal reviewed.

Operational playbooks (short):
- Incident: if carveout activation causes systemic latency regressions, STA will auto-disable new carveouts and schedule a warm-pool scale-out. Ops person should: 1) identify tenant(s) via dashboard, 2) toggle offending entitlements to soft-lease, 3) notify tenant success team.
- Billing dispute: if tenant contests a carveout promotion-to-reserve, reconcile activation logs and ramp profile; apply credits if instrumentation gap found.

Open questions / risk areas:
- Hard vs soft economics: how many customers will choose hard-lease (expensive) vs soft-lease? We need pricing elasticity experiments.
- Complexity of admission logic: STA adds another decision surface — how do we validate correctness and avoid oscillation? Consider a PID-like ramp controller with damping.
- Cross-region failovers: performance and data egress cost tradeoffs for automatic failover need legal/finance review.
- Abuse vector: tenants might programmatically trigger many short carveouts to game availability — need rate-limiting and fraud detection.

Metrics to track:
- Carveout acceptance rate, average ramp time, fractional CPU/GPU dedicated to carveouts, P99 impact attributable to carveouts, number of declined activations, billing uplift, tenant penalty scores.

MVP checklist:
- [ ] STA admission library (simulator + run mode)
- [ ] Entitlement CRUD API + activation endpoint
- [ ] Soft-lease scheduler weights + basic priority queue
- [ ] Basic telemetry + console heatmap
- [ ] Phase 0 staging experiment runbook

Appendix: quick sequence example
1) Tenant activates 5m, +25% QPS soft-carveout at 09:12. STA checks headroom=68% (< T_warn) -> immediate acceptance, soft-weight applied.
2) At 09:14 other traffic surges; headroom drops to 78% -> STA throttles new activations and slows ramp of the 25% weight; carveout still runs but at 12% effective multiplier until headroom recovers.
3) If headroom exceeds T_hard, STA can either downgrade the carveout to 5% multiplier or failover some requests to a lower-fidelity model as per tenant fallback preference.

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus feedback on: acceptable thresholds for T_warn/T_hard, economics assumptions for hard-lease vs soft-lease, and the UX for tenant penalty remediation.
- If we like this direction, next step is a small-scale simulation (team: applied-ml + serving-runtime) and a pricing experiment owner in finance.

Contact: Priya Desai (product lead), priya@redwood.example
